catalog_quote: Stress is characterized by the loudness of a particular syllable. Stress in Subanon is not contrastive. However, there is a primary and a secondary stress in this language. The symbol [´] is used for primary stress, and the symbol [`] for secondary stress. Both are marked above the vowel that bears them. Primary stress is typically on the penultimate syllable in both unaffixed and affixed words and in compound words. ... The maximum number of syllables in unaffixed words is four. ... Following affixation, either by prefixation or suffixation, the primary stress shows consistency. It is always marked on the penultimate syllable. The secondary stress is only marked in words of four or more syllables. It falls on the alternate syllable of the syllable bearing the primary stress. ... (4) Stress positions a. Penultimate stress in disyllabic words ... ‘fishhook’ bóng.git mog.bóng.git bong.gí.ton bòng.gi.tá.nan ... b. Penultimate stress in trisyllabic words ... ‘rudder’ bon.sá.lan mòg.bon.sá.lan bòn.sa.lá.nan bon.sà.la.ná.nan ... c. Penultimate primary stress and secondary stress in quadrisyllabic words ... ‘butterfly’ kò.lom.bá.ngoy ko.lom.bà.ngoy.á.nan ... ‘gecko’ tò.gi.lók.tok to.gi.lòk.to.ká.nan.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: copies we hold (563 pp., the PDF's metadata gives the Title 'Western Subanon Grammar', Author Sharon Bulalang; OAPEN open-access copy, CC BY-NC-ND per chapter footer 'doi:10.1163/9789004703056_002'). extracted text of pp. 53-54 = printed pp. 26-27, sec. 2.2.2.4 'Stress': every segment of the reported quote is present verbatim and in order ('Stress is characterized by the loudness of a particular syllable. Stress in Subanon is not contrastive. However, there is a primary and a secondary stress in this language.'.. 'Primary stress is typically on the penultimate syllable in both unaffixed and affixed words and in compound words.'.. 'The maximum number of syllables in unaffixed words is four.'…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress is non-contrastive and fixed on the penultimate syllable of the (affixed or unaffixed, simple or compound) word; suffixation shifts it rightward so it stays penultimate (bóng.git 'fishhook' -> bong.gí.ton -> bòng.gi.tá.nan).
new_statements.secondary_stress: Only in words of four or more syllables; falls on alternate syllables counting leftward from the primary (i.e. on the pre-antepenult: kò.lom.bá.ngoy 'butterfly', bon.sà.la.ná.nan 'rudders'); for compounds described as 'on the syllable before the prepenultimate syllable'.
new_statements.exceptions: None listed; the hedge 'typically' in the first sentence is followed by 'always marked on the penultimate syllable' for affixed forms, and no counter-examples (e.g. final stress) are given. Stress explicitly stated to be non-contrastive.
new_statements.domain_note: Domain is the morphological word including prefixes, suffixes (-on, -an, -anan) and compounds; examples are citation forms syllabified with stress marks. Author is a native speaker; data from Malayal/Siocon/Gutalac-Dicolom dialect speakers, dialect differences said to be mainly lexical.
new_statements.identity_note: Source describes Western Subanon [suc] = Siocon Subanon (glottocode west2557) as a whole; author (native speaker, Malayal) draws on speakers of all three dialects (Molayal, Siocon, Gutalac-Dicolom Sinubanon) and says dialect variation is mainly lexical. The language is called simply 'Subanon' throughout the book; not to be confused with Central/Southern/Northern/Eastern Subanen or Kolibugan. Estioca 2020 (dissertation) and Bulalang 2025 (Brill book) are the same author (Sharon Joy Bulalang Estioca); Glottolog lists the dissertation twice under both surnames.

sources.note: Sec. 2.2.2.4 'Stress', pp. 26-27: stress is not contrastive; primary stress on the penultimate syllable in unaffixed, affixed (prefixed or suffixed) and compound words ('always marked on the penultimate syllable' after affixation); secondary stress only in words of 4+ syllables, on the alternate syllable from the primary (e.g. bong.gi'.ton -> bo`ng.gi.ta'.nan); same rule restated for compound nouns (3.2.4, p. 60) and compound verbs (3.3.3).
